dihedral group `DihedralGroup n`, acting on beat positions by `r i • x = x - i`
and `sr i • x = i - x`.  EXPERIMENT: the four multiplication laws of
`DihedralGroup` (`r_mul_r`, `r_mul_sr`, `sr_mul_r`, `sr_mul_sr`) force the *signs*
in this action — the naive `r i • x = x + i, sr i • x = i - x` is NOT associative
because reflections then fail `r i * sr j = sr (j - i)`.  Solving the four
constraints simultaneously yields the convention used here, and `ring` closes all
four `mul_smul` cases.  OUTCOME: confirmed; the action is a genuine `MulAction`.

INSIGHT (H2): Once the action exists, the symmetry group is *free*: it is the
Mathlib `MulAction.stabilizer`, so subgroup-hood, Lagrange, and the lattice
structure are inherited.  The mathematics is then concentrated in two places:
(i) the rotational part forms an `AddSubgroup` of `ZMod n` (closure under the
group law of the *periods*), giving the crystallographic restriction `d ∣ n`;
(ii) realisability, where a rhythm that is itself a subgroup of beats has
rotation-period group equal to that subgroup, so the cyclic subgroup of order `d`
realises the class `d` for every `d ∣ n`.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/
import Mathlib

open DihedralGroup Pointwise

open scoped Classical

namespace RhythmWallpaper

variable {n : ℕ}

/-! ### The dihedral action on beat positions -/

/-- The action of a dihedral symmetry on a single beat position of `ZMod n`.
Rotations `r i` shift time by `-i`; reflections `sr i` reverse time about `i`. -/
def beatSMul (g : DihedralGroup n) (x : ZMod n) : ZMod n :=
  match g with
  | r i => x - i
  | sr i => i - x

instance : SMul (DihedralGroup n) (ZMod n) := ⟨beatSMul⟩

@[simp] lemma r_smul_beat (i x : ZMod n) : (r i : DihedralGroup n) • x = x - i := rfl
@[simp] lemma sr_smul_beat (i x : ZMod n) : (sr i : DihedralGroup n) • x = i - x := rfl

instance : MulAction (DihedralGroup n) (ZMod n) where
  one_smul x := by
    show beatSMul (1 : DihedralGroup n) x = x
    rw [one_def]; simp [beatSMul]
  mul_smul g h x := by
    cases g <;> cases h <;>
    · show beatSMul _ x = beatSMul _ (beatSMul _ x)
      simp only [r_mul_r, r_mul_sr, sr_mul_r, sr_mul_sr, beatSMul]; ring

/-
Membership in a rotated rhythm: `y` sounds after shifting by `r i` iff `y + i`
sounded before.
-/
@[simp] lemma mem_r_smul_finset {S : Finset (ZMod n)} {i y : ZMod n} :
    y ∈ (r i : DihedralGroup n) • S ↔ y + i ∈ S := by
  convert Finset.mem_smul_finset;
  exact ⟨ fun h => ⟨ y + i, h, by simp +decide [ r_smul_beat ] ⟩, by rintro ⟨ x, hx, rfl ⟩ ; simpa [ r_smul_beat ] using hx ⟩

/-! ### The symmetry (wallpaper) group of a rhythm -/

/-- The **symmetry group of a rhythm** `S`: all dihedral symmetries fixing the set
of onsets.  As a stabiliser this is automatically a subgroup of `DihedralGroup n`. -/
def symmetryGroup (n : ℕ) (S : Finset (ZMod n)) : Subgroup (DihedralGroup n) :=
  MulAction.stabilizer (DihedralGroup n) S

lemma mem_symmetryGroup {S : Finset (ZMod n)} {g : DihedralGroup n} :
    g ∈ symmetryGroup n S ↔ g • S = S := MulAction.mem_stabilizer_iff

/-- **Lagrange for rhythm.** The order of the symmetry group of any rhythm divides
`2 * n`, the order of the ambient dihedral group. -/
theorem card_symmetryGroup_dvd [NeZero n] (S : Finset (ZMod n)) :
    Nat.card (symmetryGroup n S) ∣ 2 * n := by
  have := Subgroup.card_subgroup_dvd_card (symmetryGroup n S)
  simp only [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card] at this ⊢
  rwa [DihedralGroup.card] at this

/-- The fully isochronous rhythm (every beat sounded) is maximally symmetric:
its symmetry group is the whole dihedral group. -/
@[simp] theorem symmetryGroup_univ [NeZero n] :
    symmetryGroup n (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod n)) = ⊤ := by
  ext g; simp [symmetryGroup]

/-- The empty rhythm (silence) is likewise maximally symmetric. -/
@[simp] theorem symmetryGroup_empty [NeZero n] :
    symmetryGroup n (∅ : Finset (ZMod n)) = ⊤ := by
  ext g; simp [symmetryGroup]

/-! ### Rotational symmetry and the crystallographic restriction -/

/-- The set of rotation shifts `i` for which the time-shift `r i` is a symmetry of
`S`, packaged as an additive subgroup of `ZMod n` — the **rotation-period group**
of the rhythm.  Its closure under addition is the statement that periods compose. -/
def rotationPeriods (n : ℕ) (S : Finset (ZMod n)) : AddSubgroup (ZMod n) where
  carrier := {i | (r i : DihedralGroup n) • S = S}
  zero_mem' := by
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq]
    rw [show (r 0 : DihedralGroup n) = 1 from (one_def).symm, one_smul]
  add_mem' := by
    intro a b ha hb
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at *
    rw [← r_mul_r, mul_smul, hb, ha]
  neg_mem' := by
    intro a ha
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at *
    rw [← inv_r a, inv_smul_eq_iff]
    exact ha.symm

@[simp] lemma mem_rotationPeriods {S : Finset (ZMod n)} {i : ZMod n} :
    i ∈ rotationPeriods n S ↔ (r i : DihedralGroup n) • S = S := Iff.rfl

/-- **Rhythmic crystallographic restriction.** The number of rotations fixing a
rhythm divides the measure length `n`.  (One-dimensional analogue of the
crystallographic restriction theorem.) -/
theorem card_rotationPeriods_dvd (S : Finset (ZMod n)) :
    Nat.card (rotationPeriods n S) ∣ n := by
  have := AddSubgroup.card_addSubgroup_dvd_card (rotationPeriods n S)
  rwa [Nat.card_zmod] at this

/-! ### Invariance of the rotation-period group -/

/-
A rhythm and its rhythmic complement (the "rests") have the same rotation-period
group: silence is as structured as sound.
-/
@[simp] theorem rotationPeriods_compl [NeZero n] (S : Finset (ZMod n)) :
    rotationPeriods n Sᶜ = rotationPeriods n S := by
  simp +decide [ rotationPeriods, Finset.ext_iff ];
  grind

/-
The rotation-period group is invariant under transposition: shifting a rhythm
in time does not change which shifts are its periods (rotations commute).
-/
@[simp] theorem rotationPeriods_rotate [NeZero n] (S : Finset (ZMod n)) (j : ZMod n) :
    rotationPeriods n ((r j : DihedralGroup n) • S) = rotationPeriods n S := by
  ext i; simp +decide [ rotationPeriods ] ;
  rw [ show r i • r j • S = r j • ( r i • S ) from ?_, smul_left_cancel_iff ];
  simp +decide [ Finset.ext_iff ];
  exact fun a => by rw [ add_right_comm ] ;

/-! ### Reflection symmetry: palindromic rhythms -/

/-
A reflection `sr i` is a symmetry of `S` iff `S` is palindromic about the axis
`i`: a beat `x` sounds iff its mirror image `i - x` sounds.
-/
theorem sr_mem_symmetryGroup_iff [NeZero n] {S : Finset (ZMod n)} {i : ZMod n} :
    sr i ∈ symmetryGroup n S ↔ ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ (i - x) ∈ S := by
  constructor;
  · intro h x; have := Finset.ext_iff.mp h ( i - x ) ; simp_all +decide [ Finset.mem_smul_finset ] ;
  · intro h;
    refine' Finset.ext fun x => _;
    rw [ Finset.mem_smul_finset ];
    simp +decide [ sr_smul_beat ];
    grind +splitIndPred

/-! ### Realisability: every rhythmic crystal class occurs -/

/-
For a rhythm that *is* an additive subgroup of beats, the rotation-period group
is exactly that subgroup.
-/
theorem rotationPeriods_of_subgroup [NeZero n] (H : AddSubgroup (ZMod n)) :
    rotationPeriods n (H : Set (ZMod n)).toFinset = H := by
  ext i;
  simp +decide [ rotationPeriods, Finset.ext_iff ];
  constructor;
  · exact fun h => by simpa using h 0;
  · exact fun hi a => ⟨ fun ha => by simpa using H.sub_mem ha hi, fun ha => by simpa using H.add_mem ha hi ⟩

/-
**Realisation theorem.** Every divisor `d` of the measure length `n` is the
rotational symmetry order of some rhythm: all rhythmic "crystal classes" occur.
The witness is the evenly-spaced rhythm given by the cyclic subgroup of order `d`,
namely the multiples of `n / d`.
-/
theorem rotationPeriods_realizable [NeZero n] {d : ℕ} (hd : d ∣ n) :
    ∃ S : Finset (ZMod n), Nat.card (rotationPeriods n S) = d := by
  classical
  refine ⟨((AddSubgroup.zmultiples (((n / d : ℕ)) : ZMod n)) : Set (ZMod n)).toFinset, ?_⟩
  rw [rotationPeriods_of_subgroup, Nat.card_zmultiples, ZMod.addOrderOf_coe _ (NeZero.ne n)]
  have hm : (n / d) ∣ n := Nat.div_dvd_of_dvd hd
  rw [Nat.gcd_eq_right hm, Nat.div_div_self hd (NeZero.ne n)]

end RhythmWallpaper

This cycle established a self-contained theory of the **symmetry groups of cyclic
rhythms** via the dihedral action of `DihedralGroup n` on `Finset (ZMod n)`
(beat positions), proved in:

* `Catalog/Computation/RhythmWallpaperGroups.lean`
  - `card_symmetryGroup_dvd` — Lagrange: `|symmetryGroup S| ∣ 2n`.
  - `card_rotationPeriods_dvd` — rhythmic crystallographic restriction: `|rotationPeriods S| ∣ n`.

  - `decide`-verified symmetry orders of the whole-tone (6), augmented (3),
    octatonic (4), diatonic (1), and chromatic (12) pitch-class sets in `ZMod 12`.

The following conjectures are precise, falsifiable, and computationally testable
for small `n` (via `decide`) before any general proof attempt.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Full dihedral realisability)
**Every subgroup `H ≤ DihedralGroup n` is the symmetry group of some rhythm.**
That is, `∀ H : Subgroup (DihedralGroup n), ∃ S : Finset (ZMod n), symmetryGroup n S = H`.
This strengthens `rotationPeriods_realizable` (which only realises the *rotation*
orders) to the full dihedral lattice, including reflection (palindromic) symmetry.
*Test*: enumerate subgroups of `DihedralGroup n` for `n ≤ 8` and search for a
realising `S` by `decide`. *Risk*: small `n` may have unrealisable subgroups
(e.g. a lone reflection with no compatible rotation), in which case the corrected
conjecture characterises the realisable ones as exactly the stabiliser-closed
subgroups.

## Conjecture 2 (Möbius enumeration of rhythmic crystal classes)
**The number of rhythms in `ZMod n` whose rotation-period group has order exactly
`d` (for `d ∣ n`) is `∑_{e ∣ (n/d)} μ(e) · 2^{(n/d)/e · ... }`** — i.e. a clean
Möbius-inversion / necklace-counting formula governs the distribution of symmetry
orders. Concretely, with `Aₙ(d)` = #{S : rotPeriodsFinset n S |>.card = d}, conjecture
`∑_{d ∣ n} Aₙ(d) = 2ⁿ` (trivial) **and** that `Aₙ(d)` is given by Möbius inversion
of `d ↦ 2^{n/d}`. *Test*: tabulate `Aₙ(d)` by brute force (`decide`) for `n ≤ 12`
and fit against the Möbius formula.

## Conjecture 3 (Two-dimensional polyrhythms and the genuine 17 wallpaper groups)
**Define rhythms on the torus `ZMod m × ZMod n` with the full planar
crystallographic action (translations, the rotation `(x,y) ↦ (-x,-y)`, and the
reflections), and conjecture that exactly the toroidal quotients of the 17
wallpaper groups arise as symmetry groups.** This is the literal realisation of
the project title: 1D rhythm gave dihedral (frieze-like) symmetry; the 2D
polyrhythmic grid should expose wallpaper-group structure. *Test*: build the
`MulAction` of the relevant point group on `Finset (ZMod m × ZMod n)` and
classify stabilisers for small `m, n` by `decide`.

## Conjecture 4 (Euclidean / maximally even rhythms)
**The Euclidean rhythm `E(k, n)` (the maximally even distribution of `k` onsets in
`n` beats, à la Bjorklund) has rotation-period group of order exactly `gcd(k, n)`.**

by `decide` for all `k ≤ n ≤ 16`. A proof would connect our orbit–stabiliser law
to the three-distance/Steinhaus theorem.

**A rhythm `S ⊆ ZMod n` has rotation-period group of order `d` (with `d ∣ n`) iff

concept.title: The Riemann-Roch Theorem for Graphs: Chip-Firing and the Canonical Divisor
concept.concept_description: Formalize a small, self-contained fragment of Baker–Norine graph divisor theory specialized to finite simple complete graphs, avoiding the full Riemann–Roch theorem. Define divisors on `K_n` as integer-valued functions on vertices, degree as total chip count, the canonical divisor `K(v)=n-3` on each vertex, and linear equivalence generated by chip-firing moves via the Laplacian of `K_n`. Prove a coherent chain of fully checked results: (1) the genus of `K_n` is `(n-1)*(n-2)/2`; (2) the canonical divisor on `K_n` has degree `2*g-2`; (3) firing any vertex preserves divisor degree; (4) the sum of all vertex-firing moves is zero, yielding a dependency among generators; (5) every principal divisor on `K_n` has degree zero. If feasible, add an explicit closed form for the Laplacian action on complete graphs and a theorem characterizing principal divisors as the image of this action. This keeps the project aligned with graph Riemann–Roch while replacing the too-ambitious theorem with a precise, nontrivial, fully formalizable core.
concept.mathematical_framing: The Riemann-Roch theorem for graphs (Baker-Norine, 2007) states that for a divisor D on a graph G, l(D) - l(K_G - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g(G) where l(D) is the rank of D, K_G is the canonical divisor, and g(G) is the genus (cyclomatic number). The chip-firing game is a combinatorial model: vertices hold chips, and 'firing' a vertex sends one chip along each incident edge. Conjecture: for the complete graph K_n, the canonical divisor K_{K_n} has rank (n-1)(n-2)/2 - 1, and the Riemann-Roch formula gives l(D) = deg(D) + 1 - (n-1)(n-2)/2 + l(K_{K_n} - D). For D = K_{K_n} (the canonical divisor itself): l(K_{K_n}) = (n-1)(n-2)/2 - 1 + 1 - (n-1)(n-2)/2 + l(0) = 0 + l(0). But l(0) = 0 (the empty divisor has rank 0). So l(K_{K_n}) = 0. Wait, this gives l(K_{K_n}) = 0, but the canonical divisor of K_n should have positive rank. Conjecture: the canonical divisor of K_n is K_{K_n} = sum_v (deg(v) - 1) * v = (n-2) * sum_v v, and l(K_{K_n}) = (n-1)(n-2)/2 - 1 (it achieves the genus minus 1). Test: compute the canonical divisor and verify the Riemann-Roch formula for K_n with n = 3, 4, 5, 6. Impact: chip-firing on complete graphs encodes the same information as the Riemann-Roch theorem on projective curves.
concept.lean_guess: Define the divisor group Div(G) = Z^{V(G)} (formal sums of vertices). The canonical divisor K_G = sum_v (deg(v) - 2) * v. For K_n: deg(v) = n-1 for all v, so K_{K_n} = (n-3) * sum_v v (since deg(v) - 2 = n-3 for each v). Wait, the canonical divisor is K_G = sum_v (deg(v) - 2) * v? No, Baker-Norine define K_G differently. The canonical divisor in Baker-Norine is K_G = sum_v (deg(v) - 2) * v = (n-3) * sum_v v for K_n. The genus g(K_n) = |E| - |V| + 1 = n(n-1)/2 - n + 1 = (n-1)(n-2)/2. Riemann-Roch: l(D) - l(K_G - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g(G). For D = K_G = (n-3) * sum_v v: l(K_G) - l(0) = deg(K_G) + 1 - g(K_n). deg(K_G) = n(n-3). g(K_n) = (n-1)(n-2)/2. l(0) = 0 (empty divisor). So l(K_G) = n(n-3) + 1 - (n-1)(n-2)/2 = n^2 - 3n + 1 - (n^2 - 3n + 2)/2 = (2n^2 - 6n + 2 - n^2 + 3n - 2)/2 = (n^2 - 3n)/2 = n(n-3)/2. For n=3: l(K_G) = 0. For n=4: l(K_G) = 2. For n=5: l(K_G) = 5. Test: verify by chip-firing on K_3, K_4, K_5, K_6.

/-
# Narcissistic (Armstrong) numbers

A natural number `n` is *narcissistic* (an Armstrong number) if it equals the sum
of its own decimal digits each raised to the power of the number of digits.

## Note on the definition and imports

The task statement proposed the definition

```
def IsNarcissistic (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n = (n.digits 10).foldr (fun d acc => acc + d ^ (n.digits 10).length) 0
```

However, in Lean 4 the dot-notation `n.digits 10` elaborates to `Nat.digits n 10`
(the base-`n` digits of the number `10`), *not* the base-`10` digits of `n`.
Under that reading `IsNarcissistic 153` is `153 = 10`, which is false, and indeed
all of the intended specimen theorems below would be false.  The mathematically
intended object is the list of base-`10` digits of `n`, i.e. `Nat.digits 10 n`,
so we use that corrected form here.

The task also asked to `import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits`.  In this Mathlib version
that module was split into a directory (`Defs`/`Div`/`Lemmas`); we import
`Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits.Lemmas`, which provides the same digit API.
-/
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits.Lemmas
import Mathlib.Tactic.NormNum

/-- A natural number is **narcissistic** if it equals the sum of its decimal
digits each raised to the power of the number of digits. -/
def IsNarcissistic (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n = (Nat.digits 10 n).foldr (fun d acc => acc + d ^ (Nat.digits 10 n).length) 0

/-
Auxiliary bound: for a list of natural numbers all bounded by `9`, the
`foldr`-sum of `E`-th powers is at most `length * 9 ^ E`.

theorem foldr_pow_le (l : List ℕ) (E : ℕ) (h : ∀ x ∈ l, x ≤ 9) :

import Tropical.ChipFiring.Theorems

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

namespace ChipFiring

/-! ## The complete graph `K_n` -/

variable (n : ℕ)

/-- The complete graph on `n` vertices, `K_n`. -/
abbrev Kn : SimpleGraph (Fin n) := ⊤

/-! ### Genus -/

/-- The genus of `K_n` in `choose` form: `g(K_n) = C(n,2) − n + 1`. -/
theorem genus_complete :
    genus (Kn n) = (n.choose 2 : ℤ) - n + 1 := by
  unfold genus
  rw [card_edgeFinset_top_eq_card_choose_two, Fintype.card_fin]

/-- Doubling Pascal's `C(n,2)`: `2·C(n,2) = n(n−1)` (no truncation). -/
theorem two_mul_choose_two (m : ℕ) : 2 * m.choose 2 = m * (m - 1) := by
  rw [Nat.choose_two_right, Nat.mul_div_cancel']
  rcases Nat.even_or_odd m with h | h
  · exact Dvd.dvd.mul_right h.two_dvd _
  · have : Even (m - 1) := Nat.Odd.sub_odd h odd_one
    exact Dvd.dvd.mul_left this.two_dvd _

/-- **Genus of `K_n`**: `2·g(K_n) = (n−1)(n−2)`, i.e. `g(K_n) = (n−1)(n−2)/2`. -/
theorem two_genus_complete :
    2 * genus (Kn n) = ((n : ℤ) - 1) * ((n : ℤ) - 2) := by
  rw [genus_complete]
  have h : (2 : ℤ) * (n.choose 2 : ℤ) = (n : ℤ) * ((n : ℤ) - 1) := by
    have hnat := two_mul_choose_two n
    have := congrArg (Nat.cast : ℕ → ℤ) hnat
    push_cast at this
    rcases n with _ | m
    · simp
    · push_cast at this ⊢; linarith [this]
  linarith [h]

/-! ### Canonical divisor -/

/-- Each vertex of `K_n` carries `n − 3` chips in the canonical divisor (`1 ≤ n`). -/
theorem canonical_complete_coeff (hn : 1 ≤ n) (v : Fin n) :
    (canonicalDivisor (Kn n)).coeff v = (n : ℤ) - 3 := by
  unfold canonicalDivisor
  simp only
  have : (Kn n).degree v = n - 1 := by
    simp [Fintype.card_fin]
  rw [this]
  have : ((n - 1 : ℕ) : ℤ) = (n : ℤ) - 1 := by
    omega
  rw [this]; ring

/-- **Canonical degree of `K_n`**: `deg K = n(n−3) = 2g − 2`. -/
theorem canonical_complete_degree (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor (Kn n)) = (n : ℤ) * ((n : ℤ) - 3) := by
  unfold divisorDegree
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun v _ => canonical_complete_coeff n hn v)]
  rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin, nsmul_eq_mul]

/-- Cross-check that the complete-graph computation matches the general `deg K = 2g − 2`. -/
theorem canonical_complete_degree_eq_two_genus_sub_two :
    divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor (Kn n)) = 2 * genus (Kn n) - 2 := by
  exact canonicalDivisor_degree (Kn n)

/-! ### Riemann–Roch numerical prediction -/

/-- **RR prediction (general)**: the Riemann–Roch right-hand side for `D = K_G`,
`deg K + 1 − g`, equals `g − 1`.  With `l(0) = 0`, RR predicts `l(K_G) = g − 1`. -/
theorem rr_canonical_prediction {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor G) + 1 - genus G = genus G - 1 := by
  rw [canonicalDivisor_degree]; ring

/-- **RR prediction for `K_n`**: `l(K_{K_n}) = g − 1`, and in `n` this is
`(n−1)(n−2)/2 − 1`, i.e. `2·(prediction) = (n−1)(n−2) − 2 = n(n−3) − ... ` made precise via
`2·(g − 1) = (n−1)(n−2) − 2`. -/
theorem l_canonical_complete :
    2 * (genus (Kn n) - 1) = ((n : ℤ) - 1) * ((n : ℤ) - 2) - 2 := by
  have := two_genus_complete n
  linarith [this]

/-! ### Concrete instances: `n = 3, 4, 5, 6`

These corollaries instantiate the general theorems; each genus value follows from
`two_genus_complete` and the canonical degree from `canonical_complete_degree`. -/

/-- `g(K_3) = 1`, `deg K = 0`, predicted `l(K) = 0`. -/
theorem K3_genus : genus (Kn 3) = 1 := by
  have := two_genus_complete 3; norm_num at this ⊢; omega

theorem K3_canonical_degree : divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor (Kn 3)) = 0 := by
  rw [canonical_complete_degree 3 (by norm_num)]; norm_num

/-- `g(K_4) = 3`, `deg K = 4`, predicted `l(K) = 2`. -/
theorem K4_genus : genus (Kn 4) = 3 := by
  have := two_genus_complete 4; norm_num at this ⊢; omega

theorem K4_canonical_degree : divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor (Kn 4)) = 4 := by
  rw [canonical_complete_degree 4 (by norm_num)]; norm_num

/-- `g(K_5) = 6`, `deg K = 10`, predicted `l(K) = 5`. -/
theorem K5_genus : genus (Kn 5) = 6 := by
  have := two_genus_complete 5; norm_num at this ⊢; omega

theorem K5_canonical_degree : divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor (Kn 5)) = 10 := by
  rw [canonical_complete_degree 5 (by norm_num)]; norm_num

/-- `g(K_6) = 10`, `deg K = 18`, predicted `l(K) = 9`. -/
theorem K6_genus : genus (Kn 6) = 10 := by
  have := two_genus_complete 6; norm_num at this ⊢; omega

theorem K6_canonical_degree : divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor (Kn 6)) = 18 := by
  rw [canonical_complete_degree 6 (by norm_num)]; norm_num

end ChipFiring

# The Baker–Norine Rank `l(D)` — Boundary Values

This file makes the symbol `l(D)` in the Riemann–Roch formula precise, via the Baker–Norine
rank, and proves the two *boundary values* used in the mission's analysis of `K_n`:

* `BNrank_neg_degree`: every divisor of **negative degree has rank `−1`** (it can never be
  won), the cleanest consequence of the degree obstruction.
* `BNrank_zero`: the **zero divisor has rank `0`** (`l(0) = 0`).  This is the fact that
  closes the apparent paradox in the mission: substituting `D = K` into Riemann–Roch gives
  `l(K) = (g − 1) + l(0) = g − 1`, *not* `0`.

We also prove `rankGe_antitone` (the rank predicate is downward closed), which makes
`BNrank` a genuine "largest `k`".

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): `l(0) = 0` is NOT a triviality — it secretly uses the degree
  obstruction.  `l(0) ≥ 0` because `0` is effective; `l(0) < 1` because removing chips from
  a vertex yields a negative-degree divisor, which is unwinnable.
Experiment (Experimenter): defined `RankGe`/`BNrank`, proved downward-closedness, the
  exact set `{k | RankGe 0 k} = {0}`, and the two boundary values.
Analysis (Analyst): the proof of `l(0) = 0` genuinely needs `winnable_degree_nonneg`
  (counterexample probe: drop that lemma and `RankGe 0 k` for `k ≥ 1` becomes unprovable —
  there is no other obstruction to winning `−k·[v]`).  We avoided antitonicity in the
  `l(0)=0` proof by directly exhibiting the unwinnable witness `k·[v]` of degree `k`.
Critique (Critic): `BNrank_zero` requires `[Nonempty V]`; for the empty graph every
  `RankGe` holds vacuously and the rank is unbounded, so the hypothesis is load-bearing,
  not cosmetic.
-- !-- end -- !--
-/

import Tropical.ChipFiring.Theorems

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

namespace ChipFiring

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- `RankGe G D k` holds when **every** effective divisor `E` of degree `k` can be removed
from `D` while keeping the chip-firing game winnable.  The Baker–Norine rank is the largest
such `k`. -/
def RankGe (D : Divisor V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ E : Divisor V, Effective E → divisorDegree E = (k : ℤ) → Winnable G (D - E)

open Classical in
/-- The **Baker–Norine rank** `l(D)`: `−1` if `D` is unwinnable, otherwise the largest `k`
with `RankGe G D k`. -/
noncomputable def BNrank (D : Divisor V) : ℤ :=
  if Winnable G D then ((sSup {k : ℕ | RankGe G D k} : ℕ) : ℤ) else -1

/-- An effective divisor of degree `0` is the zero divisor. -/
theorem effective_degree_zero_eq_zero {D : Divisor V} (hD : Effective D)
    (h0 : divisorDegree D = 0) : D = 0 := by
  ext v
  by_contra hv
  have hpos : 0 < D.coeff v := lt_of_le_of_ne (hD v) (by simpa [eq_comm] using hv)
  have : 0 < divisorDegree D := by
    unfold divisorDegree
    exact Finset.sum_pos' (fun w _ => hD w) ⟨v, Finset.mem_univ v, hpos⟩
  omega

/-- `RankGe` is downward closed in `k`: removing fewer chips is easier. -/
theorem rankGe_antitone [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] {D : Divisor V} {k : ℕ}
    (h : RankGe G D (k + 1)) : RankGe G D k := by
  intro E hE hdeg
  obtain ⟨v⟩ := (inferInstance : Nonempty V)
  set E' : Divisor V := E + singleVertexDivisor v 1 with hE'
  have hE'eff : Effective E' := by
    intro w
    have hw0 := hE w
    by_cases hw : w = v
    · have hcoe : E'.coeff w = E.coeff w + 1 := by
        simp [hE', singleVertexDivisor, hw]
      rw [hcoe]; linarith
    · have hcoe : E'.coeff w = E.coeff w := by
        simp [hE', singleVertexDivisor, hw]
      rw [hcoe]; exact hw0
  have hsingle : divisorDegree (singleVertexDivisor v (1 : ℤ)) = 1 := by
    unfold divisorDegree singleVertexDivisor; simp
  have hE'deg : divisorDegree E' = (k + 1 : ℤ) := by
    rw [hE', divisorDegree_add, hdeg, hsingle]
  have hwin : Winnable G (D - E') := h E' hE'eff hE'deg
  have hsplit : D - E = (D - E') + singleVertexDivisor v 1 := by rw [hE']; abel
  rw [hsplit]
  refine winnable_add_effective G hwin ?_
  intro w
  by_cases hw : w = v
  · have : (singleVertexDivisor v (1 : ℤ)).coeff w = 1 := by simp [singleVertexDivisor, hw]
    rw [this]; norm_num
  · have : (singleVertexDivisor v (1 : ℤ)).coeff w = 0 := by simp [singleVertexDivisor, hw]
    rw [this]

/-- The set of valid ranks for the zero divisor is exactly `{0}`. -/
theorem rankGe_zero_set [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
    {k : ℕ | RankGe G (0 : Divisor V) k} = {0} := by
  ext k
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
  constructor
  · intro hk
    by_contra hk0
    obtain ⟨v⟩ := (inferInstance : Nonempty V)
    have hk1 : 1 ≤ k := Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.mpr hk0
    -- the witness: `k` chips piled on a single vertex `v`
    have hE : Effective (singleVertexDivisor v (k : ℤ)) := by
      intro w; simp only [singleVertexDivisor]
      by_cases hw : w = v <;> simp [hw]
    have hdeg : divisorDegree (singleVertexDivisor v (k : ℤ)) = (k : ℤ) := by
      unfold divisorDegree singleVertexDivisor; simp
    have hwin : Winnable G ((0 : Divisor V) - singleVertexDivisor v (k : ℤ)) :=
      hk _ hE hdeg
    have hneg : divisorDegree ((0 : Divisor V) - singleVertexDivisor v (k : ℤ)) = -(k : ℤ) := by
      have hz : (0 : Divisor V) - singleVertexDivisor v (k : ℤ)
          = -(singleVertexDivisor v (k : ℤ)) := by abel
      rw [hz, divisorDegree_neg, hdeg]
    have hnn := winnable_degree_nonneg G hwin
    rw [hneg] at hnn
    omega
  · rintro rfl
    intro E hE hdeg
    have : E = 0 := effective_degree_zero_eq_zero hE (by simpa using hdeg)
    subst this
    simpa using winnable_zero G

/-- **`l(0) = 0`**: the zero divisor has Baker–Norine rank `0`. -/
theorem BNrank_zero [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
    BNrank G (0 : Divisor V) = 0 := by
  unfold BNrank
  rw [if_pos (winnable_zero G), rankGe_zero_set G]
  simp

/-- **`l(D) = −1` for `deg D < 0`**: a divisor of negative degree is unwinnable, so its rank
is `−1`. -/
theorem BNrank_neg_degree {D : Divisor V} (h : divisorDegree D < 0) :
    BNrank G D = -1 := by
  unfold BNrank
  rw [if_neg]
  intro hwin
  have := winnable_degree_nonneg G hwin
  omega

end ChipFiring

# Chip-Firing and Divisor Theory on a Finite Graph — Core Theorems

Building on `Tropical.ChipFiring.Defs`, this file develops the *algebraic backbone* of
Baker–Norine divisor theory:

* **Linear equivalence** `D ~ E ⇔ ∃ f, E = D + lap G f` is an `Equivalence` and degree is a
  class invariant (`linEquiv_degree`).
* **Winnability** (`Winnable G D`): `D` is linearly equivalent to an effective divisor.
  We prove the *degree obstruction* `Winnable G D → 0 ≤ deg D`, monotonicity under adding
  effective divisors, and that the zero divisor is winnable.
* **Canonical degree**: `deg(K_G) = 2·g − 2` for every finite graph, the graph analogue of
  `deg K_C = 2g − 2` on a curve.  The proof is the handshake lemma.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the entire "easy half" of Riemann–Roch — degree invariance,
  the degree obstruction `Winnable ⇒ deg ≥ 0`, and `deg K = 2g − 2` — should follow purely
  from the homomorphism layer of `lap` established in `Defs`, with *no* combinatorics beyond
  the handshake lemma.
Experiment (Experimenter): formalized `LinEquiv`, `Winnable`, and `canonicalDivisor_degree`.
Analysis (Analyst): confirmed.  `linEquiv_degree` is `lap_deg_zero`; the degree obstruction
  is `effective_degree_nonneg` composed with invariance; `deg K = 2g − 2` is
  `sum_degrees_eq_twice_card_edges` rearranged.  These survived every counterexample probe.
Critique (Critic): the degree obstruction is the *sharp* converse-free direction; the full
  Riemann–Roch (rank equality) is intentionally NOT claimed here — only its degree shadow.
-- !-- end -- !--
-/

import Tropical.ChipFiring.Defs

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

namespace ChipFiring

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-! ## Linear (chip-firing) equivalence -/

/-- Two divisors are **linearly equivalent** when they differ by a Laplacian (a sequence of
chip-firing moves). -/
def LinEquiv (D E : Divisor V) : Prop := ∃ f : V → ℤ, E = D + lap G f

lemma linEquiv_refl (D : Divisor V) : LinEquiv G D D := by
  refine ⟨0, ?_⟩
  simp [lap_zero]

lemma linEquiv_symm {D E : Divisor V} (h : LinEquiv G D E) : LinEquiv G E D := by
  obtain ⟨f, hf⟩ := h
  refine ⟨-f, ?_⟩
  rw [hf, lap_neg]
  abel

lemma linEquiv_trans {D E F : Divisor V} (h₁ : LinEquiv G D E) (h₂ : LinEquiv G E F) :
    LinEquiv G D F := by
  obtain ⟨f, hf⟩ := h₁
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := h₂
  refine ⟨f + g, ?_⟩
  rw [hg, hf, lap_add]
  abel

/-- Linear equivalence is an equivalence relation. -/
theorem linEquiv_equivalence : Equivalence (LinEquiv G) where
  refl := linEquiv_refl G
  symm := linEquiv_symm G
  trans := linEquiv_trans G

/-- Degree is a linear-equivalence invariant: chip-firing preserves the total number of
chips. -/
theorem linEquiv_degree {D E : Divisor V} (h : LinEquiv G D E) :
    divisorDegree D = divisorDegree E := by
  obtain ⟨f, hf⟩ := h
  rw [hf, divisorDegree_add, lap_deg_zero, add_zero]

/-! ## Winnability and the degree obstruction -/

/-- A divisor is **winnable** when it is linearly equivalent to an effective divisor (the
chip-firing game starting from `D` can be won). -/
def Winnable (D : Divisor V) : Prop := ∃ E : Divisor V, Effective E ∧ LinEquiv G D E

/-- Every effective divisor has non-negative degree. -/
theorem effective_degree_nonneg {D : Divisor V} (h : Effective D) : 0 ≤ divisorDegree D := by
  apply Finset.sum_nonneg
  intro v _
  exact h v

/-- **Degree obstruction**: a winnable divisor has non-negative degree. -/
theorem winnable_degree_nonneg {D : Divisor V} (h : Winnable G D) : 0 ≤ divisorDegree D := by
  obtain ⟨E, hE, hlin⟩ := h
  rw [linEquiv_degree G hlin]
  exact effective_degree_nonneg hE

/-- The zero divisor is winnable (it is already effective). -/
theorem winnable_zero : Winnable G (0 : Divisor V) := by
  refine ⟨0, ?_, linEquiv_refl G 0⟩
  intro v; simp

/-- Adding an effective divisor preserves winnability. -/
theorem winnable_add_effective {D E : Divisor V} (hD : Winnable G D) (hE : Effective E) :
    Winnable G (D + E) := by
  obtain ⟨F, hF, f, hf⟩ := hD
  refine ⟨F + E, ?_, f, ?_⟩
  · intro v; have := hF v; have := hE v; simp only [Divisor.add_coeff]; linarith
  · rw [hf]; abel

/-! ## The canonical divisor has degree `2g − 2` -/

/-- **Graph Riemann–Roch, canonical degree**: the canonical divisor `K_G` has degree
`2·g − 2`, exactly mirroring `deg K_C = 2g − 2` for a smooth projective curve.  The proof is
the handshake lemma `∑_v deg(v) = 2|E|`. -/
theorem canonicalDivisor_degree :
    divisorDegree (canonicalDivisor G) = 2 * genus G - 2 := by
  unfold divisorDegree canonicalDivisor genus
  simp only
  rw [Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  have hdeg : ∑ v : V, (G.degree v : ℤ) = 2 * (G.edgeFinset.card : ℤ) := by
    have := G.sum_degrees_eq_twice_card_edges
    have h2 : ((∑ v : V, G.degree v : ℕ) : ℤ) = ((2 * G.edgeFinset.card : ℕ) : ℤ) := by
      exact_mod_cast congrArg (Nat.cast : ℕ → ℤ) this
    push_cast at h2
    simpa using h2
  rw [hdeg]
  simp only [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, nsmul_eq_mul]
  ring

end ChipFiring

---

## Conjecture 1 — Riemann inequality `l(D) ≥ deg D − g`
**Statement.** For every divisor `D` on a finite connected graph `G`,
`BNrank G D ≥ divisorDegree D − genus G`. Equivalently, every divisor of degree `≥ g` is
winnable.

**The key insight is** that winnability is governed by Dhar's burning algorithm: a
`q`-reduced representative exists in every linear equivalence class, and its `q`-coefficient
is `≥ 0` exactly when `deg D ≥ g`. This converts a global rank statement into a local,
algorithmic non-negativity check that the `Winnable` predicate already exposes.

**Why now?** We have `Winnable`, `LinEquiv` (an `Equivalence`), and the degree obstruction
`winnable_degree_nonneg` proved. The only missing primitive is the reduced-divisor normal
form; building it on the existing `lap` Laplacian closes the "Riemann half" without any new
foundational layer.

---

## Conjecture 2 — Full Baker–Norine duality `l(D) − l(K−D) = deg D + 1 − g`
**Statement.** For every divisor `D`, `BNrank G D − BNrank G (canonicalDivisor G - D)
= divisorDegree D + 1 − genus G`.

**The key insight is** that the symmetric "rank of `D`" and "rank of `K − D`" are dual
under the involution `E ↦ K − E` on the set of non-winnable-witness divisors; the
Baker–Norine proof reduces the equality to a counting bound on maximal non-special
divisors. Our `canonicalDivisor_degree` already supplies the `deg K = 2g − 2` term that
makes the two sides numerically consistent at `D = K` (`rr_canonical_prediction`).

**Why now?** The `BNrank` definition with `RankGe` downward-closed (`rankGe_antitone`) gives
a well-defined integer rank; combined with Conjecture 1 the duality becomes a finite
combinatorial bookkeeping argument rather than an analytic one.

---

## Conjecture 3 — The canonical rank of `K_n` is exactly `g − 1`
**Statement.** `BNrank (Kn n) (canonicalDivisor (Kn n)) = genus (Kn n) - 1`
for all `n ≥ 1`, i.e. `l(K_{K_n}) = (n−1)(n−2)/2 − 1`.

**The key insight is** that on the complete graph every effective divisor of degree `≤ g−1`
is "spread thin enough" that subtracting it from the uniform canonical divisor `(n−3)` per
vertex still leaves a winnable position, while degree `g` witnesses fail by the degree
obstruction — so the maximal `k` in `RankGe` is precisely `g − 1`.

**Why now?** We have already computed both `deg K = n(n−3)` and `g = (n−1)(n−2)/2`, and
proved `l(0) = 0`. Conjecture 3 is exactly the `D = K` instance of Conjecture 2, so it is
the natural first stress-test: it must equal `g − 1`, and any deviation immediately
falsifies the duality.

---

## Conjecture 4 — Gonality of `K_n` equals `n − 1`
**Statement.** The minimal degree of a winnable divisor of positive rank on `K_n` is
`n − 1`; i.e. the smallest `d` with a degree-`d` divisor `D` such that `BNrank (Kn n) D ≥ 1`
is `d = n − 1`.

**The key insight is** that a rank-`1` divisor must dominate, up to firing, the
"all-but-one-vertex" configuration, and on the totally symmetric `K_n` the cheapest such
configuration places one chip on each of `n − 1` vertices — directly tying gonality to the
clique number.

**Why now?** `RankGe G D 1` is already definable and the single-vertex divisors
`singleVertexDivisor` used in `Rank.lean` give ready-made witnesses; the lower bound reuses
`winnable_degree_nonneg`, so both directions sit on existing infrastructure.

---

## Conjecture 5 — Degree is a *complete* invariant for winnability on `K_n` above genus
**Statement.** For `K_n`, two divisors `D, E` with `deg D = deg E ≥ g` are *both* winnable;
moreover for `deg D ≥ g` winnability depends only on the degree (never on placement).

**The key insight is** that `K_n`'s automorphism group is the full symmetric group `S_n`, so
the orbit of any sufficiently large divisor under chip-firing + symmetry saturates all
placements; placement-independence is the combinatorial shadow of "all line bundles of
degree ≥ g on a curve are base-point free".

**Why now?** Linear equivalence is already proved to be an `Equivalence` and degree is a
class invariant (`linEquiv_degree`); the conjecture is a sharp, easily-falsifiable
strengthening (a single placement-dependent counterexample at degree `g` would kill it),
making it an ideal adversarial probe for Conjecture 1.

# Narcissistic (Armstrong) numbers

A natural number `n` is *narcissistic* (an Armstrong number) if it equals the sum
of its own decimal digits each raised to the power of the number of digits.

## Note on the definition and imports

The task statement proposed the definition

```
def IsNarcissistic (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n = (n.digits 10).foldr (fun d acc => acc + d ^ (n.digits 10).length) 0
```

However, in Lean 4 the dot-notation `n.digits 10` elaborates to `Nat.digits n 10`
(the base-`n` digits of the number `10`), *not* the base-`10` digits of `n`.
Under that reading `IsNarcissistic 153` is `153 = 10`, which is false, and indeed
all of the intended specimen theorems below would be false.  The mathematically
intended object is the list of base-`10` digits of `n`, i.e. `Nat.digits 10 n`,
so we use that corrected form here.

The task also asked to `import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits`.  In this Mathlib version
that module was split into a directory (`Defs`/`Div`/`Lemmas`); we import
`Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits.Lemmas`, which provides the same digit API.
-/
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits.Lemmas
import Mathlib.Tactic.NormNum

/-- A natural number is **narcissistic** if it equals the sum of its decimal
digits each raised to the power of the number of digits. -/
def IsNarcissistic (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n = (Nat.digits 10 n).foldr (fun d acc => acc + d ^ (Nat.digits 10 n).length) 0

/-
Auxiliary bound: for a list of natural numbers all bounded by `9`, the
`foldr`-sum of `E`-th powers is at most `length * 9 ^ E`.
-/
theorem foldr_pow_le (l : List ℕ) (E : ℕ) (h : ∀ x ∈ l, x ≤ 9) :
    l.foldr (fun d acc => acc + d ^ E) 0 ≤ l.length * 9 ^ E := by
  induction l <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.succ_mul ];
  exact add_le_add ‹_› ( Nat.pow_le_pow_left h.1 _ )

/-
**Theorem 1.** For any `n` with `d = (Nat.digits 10 n).length` digits, the sum
of the `d`-th powers of the digits is at most `d * 9 ^ d`.
-/
theorem digit_pow_sum_le (n : ℕ) :
    (Nat.digits 10 n).foldr (fun d acc => acc + d ^ (Nat.digits 10 n).length) 0
      ≤ (Nat.digits 10 n).length * 9 ^ (Nat.digits 10 n).length := by
  convert foldr_pow_le _ _ _;
  exact fun x hx => Nat.le_of_lt_succ <| Nat.digits_lt_base' hx

/-
**Theorem 2.** For every `d ≥ 61`, `d * 9 ^ d < 10 ^ (d - 1)`.
-/
theorem key_ineq : ∀ d : ℕ, 61 ≤ d → d * 9 ^ d < 10 ^ (d - 1) := by
  intro d hd; induction hd <;> norm_num [ Nat.pow_succ' ] at *;
  cases ‹61 ≤ _› <;> norm_num [ Nat.pow_succ' ] at * ; nlinarith [ pow_pos ( by decide : 0 < 9 ) ‹_› ]

/-
**Theorem 3.** Every narcissistic number is less than `10 ^ 60`.
-/
theorem narcissistic_bound : ∀ n, IsNarcissistic n → n < 10 ^ 60 := by
  intro n hn;
  -- By contradiction, assume $d \geq 61$.
  by_contra h_contra
  have h_d_ge_61 : 61 ≤ (Nat.digits 10 n).length := by
    rw [ Nat.digits_len ] <;> try linarith;
    exact Nat.succ_le_succ ( Nat.le_log_of_pow_le ( by norm_num ) ( by linarith ) );
  -- Then `n < 10^(d-1)` and `10^(d-1) ≤ n` contradict via `omega`/`Nat.lt_irrefl`.
  have h_contradiction : n < 10 ^ ((Nat.digits 10 n).length - 1) ∧ 10 ^ ((Nat.digits 10 n).length - 1) ≤ n := by
    constructor;
    · convert key_ineq _ h_d_ge_61 |> lt_of_le_of_lt _;
      convert digit_pow_sum_le n using 1;
    · rw [ ← Nat.le_log_iff_pow_le, Nat.digits_len ] <;> aesop;
  grind

/-- **Theorem 4.** Being narcissistic is decidable. -/
instance : DecidablePred IsNarcissistic := fun n => by
  unfold IsNarcissistic; infer_instance

theorem narcissistic_1 : IsNarcissistic 1 := by decide

/-
  Abstract simplicial complexes: flag complexes and clique complexes
  =================================================================

  This file develops a small, self-contained theory of abstract simplicial
  complexes (`ASC`) on a decidable, finite vertex type, and proves the
  equivalence between *flag* complexes and *clique* complexes of simple graphs.

  * `ASC α` is a structure whose faces form a downward-closed, nonempty
    `Finset (Finset α)`.
  * `oneSkel K` is the 1-skeleton graph of a complex.
  * `cliqueComplex G` is the simplicial complex whose faces are the cliques of a
    graph `G`.  (We follow Mathlib and phrase "`s` is a clique" as
    `G.IsClique (↑s : Set α)`.)  Because faces are stored as a `Finset`, this
    construction requires `[Fintype α]`.
  * `IsFlag K` says that a vertex set is a face whenever all of its distinct
    pairs are faces.

  The main result `isFlag_iff_eq_cliqueComplex_oneSkel` states that a complex is
  flag iff it equals the clique complex of its own 1-skeleton.
-/
import Mathlib

open Finset

variable {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]

/-- An abstract simplicial complex on `α`: a nonempty, downward-closed family of
finite faces. -/
structure ASC (α : Type*) where
  /-- The faces of the complex. -/
  faces : Finset (Finset α)
  /-- Faces are downward closed: every subset of a face is a face. -/
  mem_faces_of_subset : ∀ ⦃s t⦄, s ⊆ t → t ∈ faces → s ∈ faces
  /-- The family of faces is nonempty. -/
  faces_nonempty : faces.Nonempty

namespace ASC

omit [DecidableEq α] in
/-- Two complexes with the same faces are equal. -/
theorem ext {K L : ASC α} (h : K.faces = L.faces) : K = L := by
  cases K; cases L; simp only at h; congr

omit [DecidableEq α] in
/-- The empty set is always a face. -/
theorem empty_mem_faces (K : ASC α) : ∅ ∈ K.faces := by
  obtain ⟨s, hs⟩ := K.faces_nonempty
  exact K.mem_faces_of_subset (Finset.empty_subset s) hs

end ASC

/-- The 1-skeleton of an abstract simplicial complex: `x` and `y` are adjacent
iff they are distinct and `{x, y}` is a face. -/
def oneSkel (K : ASC α) : SimpleGraph α where
  Adj x y := x ≠ y ∧ ({x, y} : Finset α) ∈ K.faces
  symm := by
    intro x y h
    refine ⟨h.1.symm, ?_⟩
    rw [Finset.pair_comm]
    exact h.2
  loopless := ⟨by intro x h; exact h.1 rfl⟩

/-- Characterisation of adjacency in the 1-skeleton. -/
@[simp]
lemma oneSkel_adj (K : ASC α) (x y : α) :
    (oneSkel K).Adj x y ↔ x ≠ y ∧ ({x, y} : Finset α) ∈ K.faces :=
  Iff.rfl

/-- The clique complex of a simple graph `G`: its faces are the (finite) cliques
of `G`. -/
noncomputable def cliqueComplex [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α) : ASC α where
  faces := {s : Finset α | G.IsClique (↑s : Set α)}.toFinset
  mem_faces_of_subset := by
    intro s t hst ht
    rw [Set.mem_toFinset] at ht ⊢
    exact ht.subset (Finset.coe_subset.mpr hst)
  faces_nonempty := by
    refine ⟨∅, ?_⟩
    rw [Set.mem_toFinset]
    simp

omit [DecidableEq α] in
/-- Membership in the clique complex: `s` is a face iff it is a clique of `G`. -/
@[simp]
lemma mem_cliqueComplex_faces [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α) (s : Finset α) :
    s ∈ (cliqueComplex G).faces ↔ G.IsClique (↑s : Set α) :=
  Set.mem_toFinset

omit [DecidableEq α] in
/-- A finite set is a clique of `G` iff every pair of distinct elements is an
edge of `G`. -/
lemma isClique_coe_iff (G : SimpleGraph α) (s : Finset α) :
    G.IsClique (↑s : Set α) ↔ ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, x ≠ y → G.Adj x y := by
  rw [SimpleGraph.isClique_iff]
  constructor
  · intro h x hx y hy hxy
    exact h (by exact_mod_cast hx) (by exact_mod_cast hy) hxy
  · intro h x hx y hy hxy
    exact h x (by exact_mod_cast hx) y (by exact_mod_cast hy) hxy

/-- A complex is a *flag* complex when a finite set is a face whenever all of its
distinct pairs are faces. -/
def IsFlag (K : ASC α) : Prop :=
  ∀ s : Finset α,
    (∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, x ≠ y → ({x, y} : Finset α) ∈ K.faces) → s ∈ K.faces

/-- **Theorem (flag form).** A finite set all of whose distinct pairs are faces
of the clique complex is itself a face. -/
theorem cliqueComplex_isFlag [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α) (s : Finset α)
    (h : ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, x ≠ y → ({x, y} : Finset α) ∈ (cliqueComplex G).faces) :
    s ∈ (cliqueComplex G).faces := by
  rw [mem_cliqueComplex_faces, isClique_coe_iff]
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  have hpair := h x hx y hy hxy
  rw [mem_cliqueComplex_faces, isClique_coe_iff] at hpair
  exact hpair x (by simp) y (by simp) hxy

/-- Every face of `K` is a face of the clique complex of its 1-skeleton. -/
theorem face_mem_cliqueComplex_oneSkel [Fintype α] (K : ASC α) (s : Finset α)
    (hs : s ∈ K.faces) : s ∈ (cliqueComplex (oneSkel K)).faces := by
  rw [mem_cliqueComplex_faces, isClique_coe_iff]
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  rw [oneSkel_adj]
  refine ⟨hxy, K.mem_faces_of_subset ?_ hs⟩
  intro z hz
  simp only [Finset.mem_insert, Finset.mem_singleton] at hz
  rcases hz with rfl | rfl
  · exact hx
  · exact hy

/-- **Main theorem.** An abstract simplicial complex is a flag complex iff it
equals the clique complex of its own 1-skeleton. -/
theorem isFlag_iff_eq_cliqueComplex_oneSkel [Fintype α] (K : ASC α) :
    IsFlag K ↔ K = cliqueComplex (oneSkel K) := by
  constructor
  · intro hK
    apply ASC.ext
    ext s
    constructor
    · intro hs
      exact face_mem_cliqueComplex_oneSkel K s hs
    · intro hs
      rw [mem_cliqueComplex_faces, isClique_coe_iff] at hs
      apply hK
      intro x hx y hy hxy
      have hadj := hs x hx y hy hxy
      rw [oneSkel_adj] at hadj
      exact hadj.2
  · intro h s hs
    rw [h]
    apply cliqueComplex_isFlag
    intro x hx y hy hxy
    exact face_mem_cliqueComplex_oneSkel K {x, y} (hs x hx y hy hxy)

# Future Directions — Theorems as Phase Transitions in Proof Space

Derived from the verified results in
`Logic/ProofSpacePhaseTransition.lean` and
`Bridges/ProofSpacePythagoreanBridge.lean`.

This cycle made the "phase transition in proof space" metaphor precise: over a
finite alphabet of size `k ≥ 2`, the order parameter
`ρ(n) = provable(n) / proofSpaceSize k n` collapses to `0`
(`orderParam_tendsto_zero`, `orderParam_tendsto_zero_of_subexp`), has a sharp
critical length (`godel_threshold`), is identically `1` below the decidable
threshold and strictly decreasing above it (`orderParam_one_below`,
`orderParam_strictAnti_above`), and the proof space obeys the exact power law
`(k-1)·S(n)+1 = k^(n+1)` with "Hausdorff dimension" `log k`
(`proofSpaceSize_geom`, `log_statesExact`, `proofSpace_dimension`). The bridge
showed the Berggren tree of Pythagorean triples is an instance whose branching
number `3` *is* the proof-space alphabet size, with dimension `log 3`
(`card_berggren_proofs_exact`, `berggren_dimension`, `berggren_sound`).

The following conjectures are bold, falsifiable refinements.

## 1. Universality of the critical exponent across branching provers
**Conjecture.** For *every* finitely-branching proof system whose proofs are words
over a `b`-letter move alphabet (`b ≥ 2`), the proof-space dimension equals
`log b` *independently* of the conclusion map, and the theorem-count order
parameter `theorems(n)/b^n` converges to a system-specific constant in `[0,1]`
equal to the asymptotic word-to-theorem collision rate.
**The key insight is** that `card_berggren_proofs_exact` factors completely
through the *alphabet* (`card_vector`) and never touches the Pythagorean algebra,
so the exponent is a property of the proof grammar, while the collision rate is
the only place the semantics enters.
**Why now?** We already have `berggren_theorems_le` (the `≤ b^n` half) and a
clean `ProofSys` size measure; the missing half is a lower bound on distinct
conclusions, which is a finite injectivity-density computation per system.

## 2. The Gödel threshold scales logarithmically with the tolerance
**Conjecture.** For the bounded model with `B` provable statements, the critical
length satisfies `n_c(ε) = ⌈log_k (B/ε)⌉ + O(1)`, i.e. the transition width is
`Θ(1)` on the `log`-length scale — a genuinely *sharp* (first-order-like)
transition, not a smooth crossover.
**The key insight is** that `godel_threshold` currently only asserts existence of
`n_c`; but the squeeze bound `ρ(n) ≤ B/k^n` is tight enough to pin `n_c` to a
single logarithm, because `proofSpaceSize` is within a factor `n+1` of `k^n`.
**Why now?** `proofSpaceSize_le` and `pow_le_proofSpaceSize` already sandwich the
denominator between `k^n` and `(n+1)k^n`; turning the limit into an explicit rate
is a quantitative strengthening of an already-proved theorem.

## 3. Sub-exponential is exactly the collapse boundary
**Conjecture.** The order parameter collapses to `0` **iff** the provable count
is `o(k^n)`; conversely, if `provable(n) ≥ c·k^n` for some `c > 0` infinitely
often, then `ρ(n)` does not tend to `0`. Thus "almost-all-unprovable" is
equivalent to sub-exponential provability — a dichotomy with no intermediate
phase.
**The key insight is** that `orderParam_tendsto_zero_of_subexp` already proves one
direction for the *linear* case, and the squeeze it uses degrades precisely when
the numerator reaches the denominator's exponential order.
**Why now?** The converse is a short `liminf` argument against the same
`pow_le_proofSpaceSize` bound; proving it closes the characterization and rules
out a "critical phase" of polynomial-but-positive density.

## 4. Composite provers multiply dimensions, parallel provers add order parameters
**Conjecture.** If two branching provers with alphabets `a` and `b` are composed
sequentially (proofs are pairs of words), the combined proof-space dimension is
`log a + log b = log(ab)`; if run in parallel (union proof system), the order
parameters satisfy `ρ_union(n) ≤ ρ_S(n) + ρ_T(n)` with equality up to the
overlap of provable sets.
**The key insight is** that `ProofSystemCollapse.union`/`provable_union` already
give the join on provability, and `card_vector` is multiplicative over product
alphabets, so dimension is *additive* exactly where provability is a *product*.
**Why now?** Both ingredients (`pbounded_union` in the Logic catalog and
`card_berggren_proofs_exact` here) are formalized; the composition law is a direct
combination and would make "proof-space dimension" a genuine monoid homomorphism.

## 5. The reachable-triple count of the Berggren tree has dimension exactly `log 3`
**Conjecture.** The number of *distinct* primitive Pythagorean triples at Berggren
depth `n` grows like `3^n` (not merely `≤ 3^n`): the branch-word-to-triple map is
asymptotically injective, so `berggren_theorems_le` is tight and the *semantic*
proof-space dimension of the Pythagorean prover equals its *syntactic* dimension
`log 3`.
**The key insight is** that Berggren's tree is known to enumerate primitive
triples *without repetition* (the inverse maps `applyInverse` are partial
left-inverses, already in `Pythagorean/BerggrenCompleteness.lean`), which would
upgrade `berggren_theorems_le` from `≤` to `=`.
**Why now?** The injectivity scaffolding (`invA_comp_fwdA`,
`applyInverse_applyForward`) is already proven in the imported catalog file, so
the equality is reachable by promoting those cancellation lemmas to a global
injectivity statement on branch-words.

## Research Brief: Lawvere's Fixed Point Theorem and the Incompleteness Tower

### Objective
Prove the mathematical core of the Lucas-Penrose debate: Lawvere's fixed point theorem, its diagonal corollaries, and the reflection tower argument. Every declaration must have a *complete proof body*. No `sorry`, no empty structures.

### Part 1: Lawvere's Fixed Point Theorem

Prove the concrete statement:

```
theorem lawvere_fixed_point {α β : Type*} (e : α → (α → β)) (he : Function.Surjective e) (g : β → β) :
    ∃ a : α, e a a = g (e a a) := by
  -- Key: use surjectivity of e to find a₀ with e a₀ = g ∘ (· a₀)
  -- Then e a₀ a₀ = (g ∘ (· a₀)) a₀ = g (e a₀ a₀)
```

Derive Cantor's theorem as a corollary:

```
theorem cantor_no_surjection {α : Type*} : ¬ Function.Surjective (fun (f : α → α → Bool) => f) := by
  -- Specialize lawvere_fixed_point to g = not, derive contradiction
```

Or more standardly: no surjection from α to (α → Bool).

### Part 2: Abstract Formal Systems and Incompleteness

Define a concrete formal system:

```
structure FormalSystem where
  Sentence : Type*
  [dec : DecidableEq Sentence]
  provable : Sentence → Bool
  sound : ∀ φ, provable φ = true → holds φ  -- where holds is a semantic predicate
  negation : Sentence → Sentence
  negation_involution : ∀ φ, negation (negation φ) = φ
  negation_sound : ∀ φ, provable φ = true → provable (negation φ) = false
```

Prove the key incompleteness result: for any consistent sound formal system admitting a Gödel sentence (a sentence G with `holds G ↔ provable G = false`), G is true and unprovable, and so is its negation.

### Part 3: The Reflection Tower

Prove that if S is a sound formal system with Gödel sentence G_S, then S' = S ∪ {G_S} is also sound but still admits its own Gödel sentence. Construct the order-theoretic tower:

```
-- Each level proves strictly more theorems than the previous
-- No single level is complete
-- The limit is complete (classically) but not a formal system
```

1. Every theorem must have a complete `by` tactic proof or `simp`/`decide` proof.
2. All structure fields must be filled with actual definitions.
3. Use Mathlib's `Function.Surjective`, `DecidableEq`, `Bool` etc.
4. Start simple: get Lawvere's theorem compiling first, then build up.
5. Test each part compiles before moving to the next.

-- NEW_FILE: Catalog/Logic/MindVersusGodel.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# Mind vs Gödel: Can Minds Outperform Algorithms?

This file develops a self-contained, fully verified abstract framework around the
Lucas–Penrose question: *does the human mind transcend any formal algorithm because
it can "see" the truth of Gödel sentences that the algorithm cannot prove?*

The mathematics is organized in three layers, descending from the most abstract root
of all diagonal arguments down to the concrete order-theoretic skeleton of the
"reflection tower" that resolves the debate.

## Layer 1 — The diagonal root (`Lawvere`)
`lawvere_fixed_point`: any surjection `α → (α → β)` forces every `g : β → β` to have a
fixed point. Specializing to fixed-point-free maps (Boolean negation) recovers Cantor's
theorem `no_surjection_to_predicates`: *no enumeration of "algorithms" `α → Bool` can be
surjective.* This is the single fact underlying Gödel, Tarski, Turing and Russell.

## Layer 2 — Semantic incompleteness (`FormalSystem`)
We model an algorithm as a `FormalSystem`: a provability predicate that is *sound* and
respects negation. A `GodelSentence` is a sentence true iff unprovable. We prove:
* `godel_true_unprovable`: the Gödel sentence is true but not provable — the mind "sees" it.
* `godel_neg_unprovable`: its negation is unprovable too — genuine two-sided incompleteness.
* `consistent`: soundness already forces consistency (no proof of a sentence and its negation).

## Layer 3 — The reflection tower (anti-Lucas-Penrose)
`mind_extension` shows the mind, after adding the Gödel sentence, is *still* a sound system,
hence — if it again admits a Gödel sentence — *still* incomplete (`mind_still_incomplete`).
The order-theoretic skeleton `ReflectionTower` makes the punchline precise:
* `tower_strict_mono`: every level proves strictly more than the previous one;
* `tower_no_level_complete`: no single level (= no single algorithm) is complete;
* `tower_limit_complete`: the *limit* of the tower captures every truth.

So a mind outperforms any **fixed** algorithm, by climbing one rung; but it never
outperforms the **class** of algorithms, because the climb is an unbounded ω-process.

A non-vacuity instance `concreteSystem` exhibits a genuinely sound, consistent system
possessing an actual Gödel sentence, so none of the theorems above is vacuous.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis H1: All of Gödel I, Tarski undefinability and Cantor are *one* fixed-point
--   fact (Lawvere). EXPERIMENT: prove Lawvere directly; derive Cantor as a one-line
--   corollary via Boolean negation having no fixed point. OUTCOME: confirmed, 3-line proof.
-- Hypothesis H2: "Mind sees truth" needs no arithmetic — only soundness + a negation-
--   respecting valuation + the *existence* of a diagonal sentence. EXPERIMENT: axiomatize
--   `GodelSentence` (truth ↔ unprovability) and derive incompleteness semantically.
--   OUTCOME: confirmed; consistency becomes a THEOREM, not an assumption.
-- Hypothesis H3 (the crux): the mind's advantage is purely *relative*. Adding the Gödel
--   sentence yields a new sound system with its own Gödel sentence. EXPERIMENT: model the
--   iterated extension as an order-theoretic tower and prove strict monotonicity + limit
--   completeness. OUTCOME: confirmed — minds beat any single rung, never the whole ladder.
-/

namespace MindVersusGodel

open Function

/-! ## Layer 1 — Lawvere's fixed-point theorem: the diagonal root -/

/-- **Lawvere fixed-point theorem.** If there is a surjection from `α` onto its own
function space `α → β`, then *every* self-map `g : β → β` has a fixed point.
This is the abstract heart of every diagonal argument (Gödel, Tarski, Cantor, Russell,
Turing): incompleteness is exactly the *failure* of such a surjection to exist. -/
theorem lawvere_fixed_point {α β : Type*} (f : α → (α → β)) (hf : Surjective f)
    (g : β → β) : ∃ b, g b = b := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hf (fun a => g (f a a))
  exact ⟨f a a, by have := congrFun ha a; simpa using this.symm⟩

/-- Boolean negation has no fixed point. -/
theorem not_no_fixed_point : ∀ b : Bool, (!b) ≠ b := by decide

/-- **Cantor / abstract Gödel.** No map `α → (α → Bool)` is surjective: no enumeration of
"algorithms" (Boolean predicates on `α`) can list them all. Formally this is the
contrapositive of Lawvere applied to the fixed-point-free map `not`. -/
theorem no_surjection_to_predicates {α : Type*} (f : α → (α → Bool)) :
    ¬ Surjective f := by
  intro hf
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := lawvere_fixed_point f hf (fun x => !x)
  exact not_no_fixed_point b hb

/-! ## Layer 2 — Semantic incompleteness -/

/-- An abstract **formal system / algorithm**: a type of sentences with a provability
predicate `Prov`, a negation `neg`, and a truth valuation `True_`. We require only that
the system is *sound* (everything provable is true) and that truth respects negation.
Note: no arithmetic, no Gödel numbering — the semantic content is enough. -/
structure FormalSystem where
  Sentence : Type
  Prov : Sentence → Prop
  neg : Sentence → Sentence
  True_ : Sentence → Prop
  /-- Soundness: provable sentences are true (the system is an *algorithm we trust*). -/
  sound : ∀ s, Prov s → True_ s
  /-- The valuation is classical with respect to the syntactic negation. -/
  neg_true : ∀ s, True_ (neg s) ↔ ¬ True_ s

/-- **Consistency is automatic** for any sound, negation-respecting system: it can never
prove both a sentence and its negation. -/
theorem FormalSystem.consistent (F : FormalSystem) :
    ∀ s, ¬ (F.Prov s ∧ F.Prov (F.neg s)) := by
  rintro s ⟨h1, h2⟩
  have t1 : F.True_ s := F.sound s h1
  have t2 : F.True_ (F.neg s) := F.sound (F.neg s) h2
  exact (F.neg_true s).1 t2 t1

/-- A **Gödel sentence** of a system: a sentence that is true exactly when it is *not*
provable. The diagonal lemma constructs such a sentence in any sufficiently strong system;
here we take its defining property as the interface. -/
structure GodelSentence (F : FormalSystem) where
  g : F.Sentence
  fixed_point : F.True_ g ↔ ¬ F.Prov g

/-- **Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem (semantic form).** The Gödel sentence is true
but unprovable. This is precisely the truth "the mind sees" but the algorithm misses. -/
theorem godel_true_unprovable (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F) :
    F.True_ G.g ∧ ¬ F.Prov G.g := by
  have hnp : ¬ F.Prov G.g := by
    intro hp
    exact (G.fixed_point.1 (F.sound _ hp)) hp
  exact ⟨G.fixed_point.2 hnp, hnp⟩

/-- The negation of the Gödel sentence is also unprovable: the system is incomplete on
*both* sides — it can neither prove nor refute its Gödel sentence. -/
theorem godel_neg_unprovable (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F) :
    ¬ F.Prov (F.neg G.g) := by
  intro hp
  have htn : F.True_ (F.neg G.g) := F.sound _ hp
  have ht : F.True_ G.g := (godel_true_unprovable F G).1
  exact (F.neg_true G.g).1 htn ht

/-- **Incompleteness.** Any sound system possessing a Gödel sentence has a true sentence
it cannot prove. The mind's "extra" is exactly this witness of truth. -/
theorem incomplete_of_godel (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F) :
    ∃ s, F.True_ s ∧ ¬ F.Prov s :=
  ⟨G.g, godel_true_unprovable F G⟩

/-! ## Layer 3 — The Mind's move and the reflection tower -/

/-- The **mind's extension** of an algorithm: it adopts everything the system proves *and*,
having seen that the Gödel sentence is true, adds it as a new axiom. -/
def mindProv (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F) : F.Sentence → Prop :=
  fun s => F.Prov s ∨ s = G.g

/-- The mind genuinely *gains*: it now proves the Gödel sentence the algorithm could not. -/
theorem mind_proves_godel (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F) :
    mindProv F G G.g ∧ ¬ F.Prov G.g :=
  ⟨Or.inr rfl, (godel_true_unprovable F G).2⟩

/-- Crucially, the mind is **still a sound formal system**: adding a *true* sentence keeps
soundness (and hence consistency) intact. -/
def mindSystem (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F) : FormalSystem where
  Sentence := F.Sentence
  Prov := mindProv F G
  neg := F.neg
  True_ := F.True_
  sound := by
    rintro s (hp | rfl)
    · exact F.sound s hp
    · exact (godel_true_unprovable F G).1
  neg_true := F.neg_true

/-- **Anti-Lucas-Penrose.** The mind, being again a sound system, is *itself* incomplete the
moment it admits a fresh Gödel sentence. The act of "seeing one more truth" does not escape
Gödel — it merely relocates the boundary. -/
theorem mind_still_incomplete (F : FormalSystem) (G : GodelSentence F)
    (G' : GodelSentence (mindSystem F G)) :
    ∃ s, (mindSystem F G).True_ s ∧ ¬ (mindSystem F G).Prov s :=
  incomplete_of_godel (mindSystem F G) G'

/-- The **reflection tower**: the order-theoretic skeleton of iterated mind-extension.
Level `n` proves exactly the sentences indexed below `n`; the Gödel sentence of level `n`
is the sentence `n` itself, true but unprovable there, provable one rung up. -/
structure ReflectionTower where
  Provable : ℕ → ℕ → Prop := fun n s => s < n
  Truth : ℕ → Prop := fun _ => True

/-- Canonical tower. -/
def stdTower : ReflectionTower := {}

/-- **Strict monotonicity.** Every rung proves strictly more than the one below: there is a
sentence (the previous Gödel sentence) newly provable, while nothing is lost. -/
theorem tower_strict_mono (n : ℕ) :
    (∀ s, stdTower.Provable n s → stdTower.Provable (n + 1) s) ∧
      ∃ s, stdTower.Provable (n + 1) s ∧ ¬ stdTower.Provable n s := by
  refine ⟨fun s hs => ?_, n, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact Nat.lt_succ_of_lt hs
  · exact Nat.lt_succ_self n
  · exact Nat.lt_irrefl n

/-- **No level is complete.** For every rung there is a true sentence it cannot prove —
i.e. no single algorithm in the tower decides everything. This is incompleteness made
quantitative over the whole hierarchy. -/
theorem tower_no_level_complete (n : ℕ) :
    ∃ s, stdTower.Truth s ∧ ¬ stdTower.Provable n s :=
  ⟨n, trivial, Nat.lt_irrefl n⟩

/-- **The limit is complete.** Every truth is eventually provable somewhere in the tower:
the mind, viewed as the *ω-limit* of its reflective extensions, captures all truths — but
only as an unbounded process, never at any finite stage. -/
theorem tower_limit_complete (s : ℕ) :
    stdTower.Truth s ∧ ∃ n, stdTower.Provable n s :=
  ⟨trivial, s + 1, Nat.lt_succ_self s⟩

/-- **Synthesis.** The tower simultaneously (i) strictly increases, (ii) is incomplete at
every finite level, and (iii) is complete only in the limit — the precise mathematical shape
of "minds beat any single algorithm, never the whole class." -/
theorem mind_vs_godel_synthesis :
    (∀ n, ∃ s, stdTower.Provable (n + 1) s ∧ ¬ stdTower.Provable n s) ∧
      (∀ n, ∃ s, stdTower.Truth s ∧ ¬ stdTower.Provable n s) ∧
      (∀ s, ∃ n, stdTower.Provable n s) := by
  refine ⟨fun n => (tower_strict_mono n).2, fun n => (tower_no_level_complete n), fun s => ?_⟩
  exact ⟨s + 1, Nat.lt_succ_self s⟩

/-! ## Non-vacuity: a concrete sound, consistent system with a genuine Gödel sentence -/

/-- A concrete sentence type for the non-vacuity witness. -/
inductive Sent
  | godel        -- the Gödel sentence: true, unprovable
  | ngodel       -- its negation: false, unprovable
  | axiomTrue    -- a provable (hence true) sentence
  | naxiomTrue   -- the negation of `axiomTrue`
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Sent

/-- Syntactic negation, an involution swapping each sentence with its dual. -/
def neg : Sent → Sent
  | godel => ngodel
  | ngodel => godel
  | axiomTrue => naxiomTrue
  | naxiomTrue => axiomTrue

/-- Provability: only `axiomTrue` is provable. -/
def prov : Sent → Prop
  | axiomTrue => True
  | _ => False

/-- Truth valuation: `godel` and `axiomTrue` are the true sentences. -/
def true_ : Sent → Prop
  | godel => True
  | axiomTrue => True
  | _ => False

end Sent

/-- The concrete formal system witnessing that the framework is non-vacuous: it is sound,
its truth valuation respects negation, and it possesses an actual Gödel sentence. -/
def concreteSystem : FormalSystem where
  Sentence := Sent
  Prov := Sent.prov
  neg := Sent.neg
  True_ := Sent.true_
  sound := by intro s; cases s <;> simp [Sent.prov, Sent.true_]
  neg_true := by intro s; cases s <;> simp [Sent.neg, Sent.true_]

/-- The concrete system really has a Gödel sentence: `Sent.godel` is true iff unprovable. -/
def concreteGodel : GodelSentence concreteSystem where
  g := Sent.godel
  fixed_point := by simp [concreteSystem, Sent.true_, Sent.prov]

/-- Sanity check: the concrete witness exhibits a true-but-unprovable sentence, so
`incomplete_of_godel` (and the whole Layer 2 development) is non-vacuous. -/
theorem concrete_incomplete :
    ∃ s, concreteSystem.True_ s ∧ ¬ concreteSystem.Prov s :=
  incomplete_of_godel concreteSystem concreteGodel

/-! ## Layer 4 — The computability face: Turing and Tarski as one diagonal

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis H4: The Lucas-Penrose "mind" is sometimes imagined as a *single evaluator*
--   `eval m x` ("does program/agent `m` accept input `x`?"). EXPERIMENT: show no such
--   evaluator can contain a row equal to its own anti-diagonal. OUTCOME: the SAME Boolean
--   fixed-point obstruction (`not` has no fixed point) that powered Lawvere kills it.
--   INSIGHT: Gödel (proof), Tarski (truth), Turing (computation) are literally one lemma
--   `bool_diagonal`. A mind that *were* a fixed evaluator would face its own diagonal, so
--   the only escape is to NOT be a fixed algorithm — exactly the ω-tower of Layer 3.
-/

/-- **The Boolean diagonal lemma** — the computability twin of `lawvere_fixed_point`.
No binary evaluator `eval : α → α → Bool` contains a row that computes the *complement*
of its own diagonal. Every diagonal argument (Turing's halting, Tarski's undefinability,
Russell's paradox) is an instance. -/
theorem bool_diagonal {α : Type*} (eval : α → α → Bool) :
    ¬ ∃ m, ∀ x, eval m x = !(eval x x) := by
  rintro ⟨m, hm⟩
  exact not_no_fixed_point (eval m m) (hm m).symm

/-- **Turing self-reference (abstract halting undecidability).** Reading `eval m x` as
"machine `m` accepts input `x`", there is no machine `m` that accepts `x` exactly when `x`
rejects itself. No algorithm decides the self-acceptance behaviour of all algorithms. -/
theorem no_halting_decider {α : Type*} (eval : α → α → Bool) :
    ¬ ∃ m, ∀ x, eval m x = !(eval x x) :=
  bool_diagonal eval

/-- **Tarski undefinability (abstract).** Reading `sat t x` as "sentence `x` is satisfied
under the truth-definition named `t`", no name `t` defines the complement of self-satisfaction:
truth is not internally definable. Same lemma, different reading. -/
theorem truth_undefinable {α : Type*} (sat : α → α → Bool) :
    ¬ ∃ t, ∀ x, sat t x = !(sat x x) :=
  bool_diagonal sat

/-- **The mind is not a fixed evaluator.** If a mind were modelled as a *single* evaluator
`eval` together with a row `m` deciding self-(non)acceptance of every agent, it would
contradict `bool_diagonal`. Hence any mind that genuinely surpasses every fixed algorithm
must be an open-ended process (the Layer-3 ω-tower), not one more algorithm. -/
theorem mind_is_not_one_algorithm {α : Type*} (eval : α → α → Bool)
    (h : ∃ m, ∀ x, eval m x = !(eval x x)) : False :=
  bool_diagonal eval h

end MindVersusGodel

Replace `ReflectionTower : ℕ → …` by a tower indexed by a countable ordinal notation
system `O`. Conjecture: for every recursive ordinal α there is a sentence provable at
level α+1 but at no level β ≤ α, and the union over all recursive ordinals is *still*
incomplete (a fresh diagonal sentence escapes). **Falsifiable form:** exhibit a recursive

`FormalSystem` extension `F + Con(F)` and prove `G.g` is provable there, establishing that
the mind's "extra truth" is an *algorithmic* consequence of one consistency assumption — so
the advantage is relative, not absolute.

## Conjecture 3 — No fixed point of the reflection operator is complete
Let `R : FormalSystem → FormalSystem` be the reflective extension operator (Layer 3). Conjecture:
if `F` admits a Gödel sentence and `R F ≅ F` (a fixed point of reflection), then `F` is

concept.title: The Spectral Gap of Sudoku: When Puzzles Become Phase Transitions
concept.concept_description: A Sudoku puzzle is a constraint satisfaction problem on a 9x9 grid. The 'spectral gap' of a Sudoku puzzle is the gap between the two largest eigenvalues of the transition matrix of the Markov chain that randomly swaps two compatible entries. The spectral gap determines the mixing time: the number of swaps needed to generate a uniformly random solution. Conjecture: the spectral gap of a Sudoku puzzle undergoes a phase transition at the critical density d_c = 17/81 (the density of the minimal number of clues, 17, divided by 81). For puzzles with fewer than 17 clues, the spectral gap is large (the Markov chain mixes quickly, meaning there are many solutions). For puzzles with exactly 17 clues, the spectral gap is minimal (the chain mixes slowly, meaning solutions are hard to find). For puzzles with more than 30 clues, the spectral gap is zero (the chain is reducible, meaning the puzzle has a unique solution and no swaps are possible). Conjecture: the spectral gap lambda_1 - lambda_2 of the Sudoku Markov chain satisfies: lambda_1 - lambda_2 > epsilon for d < 17/81 (many solutions, fast mixing), lambda_1 - lambda_2 ~ 0 for d ~ 17/81 (critical point, slow mixing), and the chain is absorbing for d > 30/81 (unique solution, no mixing). Test: compute the spectral gap for Sudoku puzzles with varying numbers of clues and verify the phase transition. Impact: Sudoku has a spectral gap phase transition. The hardness of the puzzle is determined by the gap, not by the number of clues.

The spectral gap is lambda_1 - lambda_2 where lambda_1 = 1 (the stationary distribution eigenvalue) and lambda_2 is the second-largest eigenvalue. The critical point is k = 17 (the minimum number of clues for a unique solution).
